passage: Nursery note, Thursday. Abhinav, two, turned his whole head toward me each time I began the counting song, eyes bright, and edged closer on the mat. At lunch he took three spoonfuls of dal and rice, then turned his head away and held his lips together. I lowered the spoon and said, “All done?” He looked back at me and smiled. I put the bowl aside. He ate a banana later. 🙂 Yusuf

qa.q: How many spoonfuls did Abhinav take at lunch before turning away?
qa.a: Three spoonfuls of dal and rice.

qa.q: What might Abhinav's head turn away from the spoon mean, and what else could it be?
qa.a: He most likely felt full and content, wanting to stop, and his smile afterwards showed he was happy. It could also mean he wanted something different.
Yusuf respected the turn-away, which shows Abhinav that his signals count, and still offered food later.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel when the spoon goes down?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and understood, and be more willing to eat again at the next meal.

grounding: A toddler turns toward a caregiver to engage and turns away to end feeding, and the caregiver respects the signal.

passage: On the mud verandah, Kiran hummed an old lullaby while she plaited her own hair. Her granddaughter Salma, two, who had been playing with pebbles, turned her head toward the sound and crawled over into her lap. Kiran held a cup of warm milk to her lips. Salma took two sips and then turned her face to the wall, lips closed. Kiran waited, then set the cup on the step. “Later, then,” she said, and went on humming.

qa.q: What did Salma turn her head toward on the verandah?
qa.a: The sound of Kiran humming an old lullaby.

qa.q: What could Salma's turn to the wall mean, and what else might it be?
qa.a: It probably means she was done with the milk. It could also mean she was too warm or wanted to keep listening to the song.

qa.q: What did Kiran do that helped?
qa.a: She waited, did not push the cup and kept humming, so Salma stayed close and comfortable.

qa.q: How might Salma feel when her signal is respected?
qa.a: She may feel that turning away is enough to be heard, which builds trust that she does not have to cry to be understood. 🙂

grounding: A toddler turns toward a caregiver to engage and away to end feeding, and the caregiver respects the turn-away.
